A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support comparison despite substantial theoretical revisions and different layouts.

before.justification: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Figures 2–3 report original optimization experiments on a quartic objective and synthetic nonconvex phase retrieval, including 100 random problem instances.

after.justification: The original experiments remain, and Section 4.3 and Figure 4 add original neural-network training results on a 600-example MNIST subset.

M1.justification: The update in Equation (2), reference-function families, and connections to memoryless adaptive methods and clipping remain unchanged. Renaming separable reference functions as anisotropic and explaining equivalent clipping parameters do not change the algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 adds neural-network training on MNIST, extending coverage from a quartic toy objective and synthetic phase retrieval to learning from image data. The original tasks remain; the logistic-loss appendix is theoretical in both versions.

E2.justification: The retained phase-retrieval comparison still includes GD, β-GD, and gradient clipping. The citation attached to β-GD changes from v1's reference [9] to Chen et al. (2023), while the plotted comparator remains. The new MNIST experiment reuses gradient clipping rather than introducing another baseline.

E3.justification: The added MNIST experiment introduces a specified fully connected ReLU network, cross-entropy loss, 600 training examples, full-gradient updates, and training-loss plots over 250 iterations. Existing phase-retrieval dimensions, data generation, and method parameters remain unchanged. Explicit quartic stepsize formulas clarify previously documented settings.

E4.justification: Figure 4 adds a parameter-sensitivity study with three paired stepsize/clipping-parameter configurations for each of two preconditioners and gradient clipping. The quartic parameter sweep and 100-instance phase-retrieval robustness comparison already existed.

E5.justification: V1 displays individual phase-retrieval trajectories across 100 random instances. V2 reports their mean with one-standard-deviation bands on a logarithmic plot and explicitly describes this reporting practice. The stated number of instances remains 100.

E6.justification: Figure 4 adds a complete set of neural-network training-loss trajectories showing different transient behavior and final losses across parameter choices. Figure 2 also contains small trajectory changes while retaining its convergence trade-off. The existing phase-retrieval ranking is retained, with aggregate results replacing the individual-run display.

T1.justification: Definition 2.4 replaces a non-strict spectral bound with a strict bound plus norm-coercivity. Proposition 2.6 replaces general strong monotonicity with injectivity, supported by a new global-homeomorphism proof; the monotonicity argument survives under a symmetry assumption in Proposition D.2. Proposition 2.9 correspondingly uses injectivity. V2 also removes the convexity restriction from Proposition 2.2's conjugate statement, adds Corollary 2.11 and Proposition D.1, and revises logistic-loss and clipping derivations in Appendix D.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the same central claims: generalized anisotropic smoothness, connections to clipping and adaptive updates, and convex/nonconvex convergence guarantees. V2's explicit exclusion of momentum and moving averages clarifies restrictions already present in v1's examples.

C2.justification: V2 discusses when the new norm-coercivity requirement is mild or avoidable and clarifies applicability of the isotropic convergence assumptions. The conclusion adds extension to additive nonsmooth objectives as a research direction and explains that it is not straightforward.

D1.justification: V2 supplies a code-repository link absent from v1, documents the MNIST network widths, activations, loss, subset size, and full-gradient updates, and lists parameter choices in Figure 4. It also explicitly states the stepsize mapping used for the existing quartic experiment.

R1.justification: V2 adds connections to accelerated methods through Kim et al. (2023) and anisotropic prox-regularity and proximal interpretations through Laude (2021), alongside new proof and MNIST references. It corrects the phase-retrieval source attribution and removes the Topics in optimal transportation reference. The overall research positioning remains stable.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and much of the prose remain intact. V2 clarifies terminology and explanations, renames separable reference functions, reorganizes Appendix D, removes the contents and classification front matter, and adds acknowledgements and an impact statement.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a two-column conference layout for the main text and references, relocating and resizing existing displays. It adds Figure 4 and a smoothness-constant summary in Table 2. Figure 3 replaces individual trajectories with mean curves and shaded uncertainty bands; Figure 2 uses equivalent reciprocal-parameter legend labels.

improvement.justification: The decisive improvement is repairing a central theoretical gap: v1's Appendix B.4 infers monotonicity from eigenvalue bounds on generally nonsymmetric matrix products. V2 restricts that argument to symmetric products and develops the general sufficiency argument through injectivity with explicit additional assumptions. The code link, statistical summaries, and MNIST experiment also improve reproducibility and empirical support. Newly added Corollary 2.11 appears to reverse the required scaling, stating δL1 rather than L1/δ; this local defect remains, but does not outweigh the substantial repair to the main argument.
